summary: The note examines how space weather such as solar flares and geomagnetic storms threatens aircraft avionics, especially on high-altitude polar routes, and the economic cost of resulting disruptions. It cites several 2023 incidents and expert comments, then outlines mitigation through forecasting, shielding, redundancy and retrofitting. It closes by stressing international cooperation and continued research.
one_line: Space weather endangers aircraft avionics and causes costly flight disruptions, requiring better forecasting, hardened systems, and international cooperation.
key_facts: Space weather includes solar flares, geomagnetic storms, and ionospheric disturbances caused by the Sun and conditions in outer space.
On October 3, 2023, during heightened solar activity, airline operators reported anomalies in flight navigation systems, with spotty signals and glitches in some onboard computers.
On September 21, 2023, a transpolar flight experienced short-lived communication failures and autopilot disengagement due to a sudden geomagnetic storm.
Dr. Lisa Gomez, a space physicist, said on November 5, 2023 that "the higher the aircraft flies, the greater the exposure to charged particles that can disrupt electronic systems."
Long-haul flights often operate at high altitudes near the poles, where Earth's magnetic field offers less shielding from high-energy particles.
Space weather can disturb avionics by corrupting data links, causing power anomalies, or directly damaging hardware.
Avionics engineer Jack Hughes said on December 10, 2023 that a powerful geomagnetic storm can induce currents in circuits never designed to handle them.
On September 16, 2023, several transatlantic routes were diverted as a precaution against a forecasted solar storm, with an estimated economic impact in the millions.
Airlines CEO Martin Fisher said on October 28, 2023 that each minute of unscheduled maintenance or inspections after space weather events translates to thousands in operational costs.
Mitigation includes monitoring and forecasting with space-weather-monitoring satellites, shielding sensitive equipment, and building redundancy into critical systems.
After the events of November 2023, some airlines quickened retrofitting older aircraft with more resistant technology and adding real-time space weather information to cockpits.
ICAO and IATA are driving initiatives to standardize reporting, improve communication, and inform policy on space weather.
A summit on February 14, 2024 saw global aviation leaders underline the urgency of shared approaches to space weather.
